pending_diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS: Acute Intermittent Porphyria (AIP) THE SMOKING GUN: Port-wine colored urine upon light exposure triggered by a low-carbohydrate diet and sulfonamide antibiotic exposure PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Acute Intermittent Porphyria is an autosomal dominant metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD) in the heme biosynthesis pathway. Environmental factors such as severe carbohydrate restriction, stress, or cytochrome P450-inducing medications (like sulfonamides) induce hepatic ALAS1 enzyme activity. This leads to a massive toxic accumulation of heme precursors, specifically aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG). Elevated ALA and PBG cause autonomic neuropathies (hypertension, tachycardia, severe visceral abdominal pain), central nervous system dysfunction (hallucinations, SIADH causing severe hyponatremia, seizures), and motor neuropathy (ascending weakness). Upon exposure to light and air, excessive urinary PBG oxidizes into porphobilin, turning the urine a classic port-wine red/dark color.
